abstract: Golgi fragmentation is an early and common feature of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, whether a shared mechanism drives Golgi fragmentation across different neurodegenerative conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase Itchy homolog (ITCH) as a key regulator of proteotoxicity through its role in inducing Golgi fragmentation. Disease-associated accumulation of ITCH promotes fragmentation of both the cis- and trans-Golgi networks, disrupting protein sorting and impairing lysosomal functions. The ITCH-dependent lysosomal dysfunction compromises the clearance of misfolded proteins associated with several neurodegenerative diseases. Inhibition of ITCH protects against proteotoxicity in both mammalian neurons and Drosophila models of neurodegeneration. The accumulation of ITCH in patients with ALS and AD is attributed to up-regulation of the ubiquitin-specific protease USP11, which deubiquitinates and stabilizes ITCH. These results uncover a pathogenic pathway regulating Golgi integrity and contributing to the development of neurodegenerative diseases.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
DNA plasmids
The lentiviral vectors pLU-CMV-His-ITCH and pLU-CMV-Flag-ITCH were created by substituting the tumor necrosis factor receptor–associated factor 6 (TRAF6)–coding sequences in the pLU-CMV-TRAF6 vector (Addgene, #66923) with a Nhe I/Sal I–flanked ITCH-coding sequence, which was obtained through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification from a cDNA library of HeLa cells (Clontech, catalog number 638862). The vectors pcDNA3.1-GNPTAB (#78108), pLJM1-Tmem192-mRFP-3xHA (#134631), pLenti_CMVTRE3G_LYSET-Isoform2_Flag (#191999), MAC-CTSB (#172413), and pRK5-HA-Ubiquitin (#17608) were obtained from Addgene. Various shRNA expression vectors were obtained from MilliporeSigma. pCDNA-PR36 was generated by inserting sequences encoding 36 repeats of the polydipeptide (PR) into pCDNA3.1. The expression vectors pRK5-SOD1
G85R
and pRK5-TDP-43
M337V
have been described before (
74
–
76
). The CRISPR vector lentiCRISPRv2-USP7 containing USP7 target sequences was cloned between the BsmB I sites of lentiCRISPRv2-Puro (Addgene, #98290). The lentiviral vectors pLU-CMV-HA-BRCC36, pLU-CMV-HA-USP11, and pLU-CMV-HA-USP15 expressing various N-terminally HA-tagged USPs were generated by PCR amplification of the respective sequences from the plasmids Flag-HA-BRCC3 (Addgene, #22540), Flag-HA-USP11(Addgene, #22566), and Flag-HA-USP15 (Addgene, #22570) using Nhe I/Sal I–flanked primers and subsequent replacement of the TRAF6 coding sequence in pLU-CMV-TRAF6. The lentiviral vectors pLU-CMV-His-ITCH-CS and pLU-CMV-HA-USP11-CS were generated by insertion of a modified ITCH or USP11 sequence (coding sequence with a point mutation at Cys
318
→ Ser generated by overlap PCR) into the corresponding cloning site of pLU-CMV-TRAF6, respectively, thereby replacing the TRAF6 sequence. A bacterial expression vector for N-terminally GST-fused USP11 was cloned using the Eco RI and Not I sites in the pGEX-4T-1 vector (GE Healthcare, catalog number 28-9545-49). Similarly, pET-Flag-ITCH encoding N-terminally Flag-tagged ITCH was cloned using the Bam HI and Sal I sites in the pET28a vector (Novagen, EM69864-3). DH5α competent
Escherichia coli
(
E. coli
, Invitrogen) and Stbl3 chemically competent
E. coli
(Invitrogen) were used for plasmid transformation and extraction.
Cell lines and cell transfection
Human retinal pigment epithelial cells [RPE1; hTERT-RPE1, American Type Culture Collection (ATCC), CRL-4000] were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM)/F-12, GlutaMAX supplement (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10565042) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, A5256701); HEK293 cells (ATCC, CRL-3216) and HeLa cells (ATCC, CCL-2) were cultured in DMEM (Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A5256701); and all cell lines were authenticated by short tandem repeat analysis. Transfection was performed with a mixture of plasmid DNAs and the cationic polymer linear polyethylenimine (Polysciences, 593215) when cells reached a confluence of ~40 to 60%.
Immunoprecipitation
Cells were collected and lysed in a solution that contained the following components: protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich, P8340), 50 mM tris-HCl (with a pH of 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, and 0.2% NP-40. After incubating for 1 hour at 4°C, a brief period of sonication was performed using a microtip, followed by centrifugation of the samples at 12,000
g
for 10 min at 4°C. The resulting supernatants were then combined with a primary antibody and Protein A/G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88803), and the mixture was incubated overnight at 4°C. Then, the samples underwent five rounds of rinsing using a wash buffer composed of 50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.2% NP-40. The collected precipitates were released by IgG elution buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 21028). For Flag-based immunoprecipitation, the precipitated proteins were released from the beads using a lysis buffer containing the 3× Flag peptide (Sigma-Aldrich, catalog number F4799).
For the denaturing precipitation-immunoblotting analysis of ubiquitination, cells were treated with 300 μl of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution containing 1% SDS and boiled for 10 min. Subsequently, the lysates were diluted 1:3 using PBS and sonicated for 1 min using a microtip sonicator. The lysates were centrifuged at a speed of 12,000
g
for 10 min. The resulting supernatants were then diluted five times with PBS. These diluted supernatants were incubated with Flag-antibody beads overnight at 4°C. After five washes with PBS buffer containing 0.2% NP-40, the proteins were released from the beads using lysis buffer containing the 3× Flag peptide.
Golgi quantification
To quantify cis- and trans-Golgi structures, we conducted IF analysis on various cells using antibodies against GM130, TGN38, and TGN46. The integrity of the Golgi was assessed by classifying GM130, TGN38, and TGN46 signals into five levels. The assigned values (1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, and 0) reflect the Golgi integrity for each cell, with an intact Golgi receiving a score of 1 and a completely smeared Golgi scoring 0. Over 30 cells in each group were classified for this assessment.
Human and mouse tissues
Tau4R-AP transgenic mice have been described previously (
50
), and details of the human tissues are provided in tables S1 and S2. Tissue extracts from mouse brains, spinal cords from patients with ALS, and brains from patients with AD were prepared according to established protocols (
45
). Briefly, the tissues were first washed with cold PBS. Then, they were homogenized using glass tissue grinders in cold radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer consisting of 50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1% SDS, 100 mM sodium fluoride, 17.5 mM β-glycerophosphate, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 10% glycerol, and EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). The resulting homogenates were centrifuged at a speed of 1000
g
at 4°C for 10 min. The supernatants were further centrifuged at 16,000
g
for an additional 10 min. The final supernatants were collected and used for subsequent immunoblotting analysis.
Mass spectrometry
For the identification of the ITCH interactome, HEK293 cells were transfected with the vectors expressing Flag-tagged ITCH for 2 days. Then, the cells were collected and lysed. Flag immunoprecipitation was performed following the procedure described above. The precipitates in elution buffer (PBS containing 3× Flag peptides) were subjected to reduction, alkylation, and trypsin digestion. The resulting peptides were analyzed using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The proteomic data were searched against the SwissProt human database using MASCOT software to identify the interacting proteins. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE (
77
) partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD057324.
IF analysis
Twenty-four hours after transfection, cells were washed twice with PBS and then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 min at room temperature. Following the fixation, cells were washed three times with PBS and then permeabilized and blocked using PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) at room temperature for 1 hour. Then, the cells were incubated with the primary antibody at 4°C overnight. After three washes, cells were incubated with the fluorescently conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 hour. Last, coverslips were mounted using ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant, which contains 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
P36971
).
Cell fractionation
Cells were washed with PBS and then suspended in a cold homogenization buffer (0.25 M sucrose, 1 mM EDTA, and 10 mM Hepes, pH 7.4). The suspension was passed repeatedly through a 23-gauge syringe needle to disrupt the cells. After centrifuging the homogenates at 1000
g
for 10 min at 4°C to remove the nuclei and undisrupted cells, the supernatants were collected to isolate the membrane fractions using density gradient ultracentrifugation. Discontinuous gradients of iodixanol were prepared using OptiPrep (Accurate Chemical and Scientific, Westbury, NY), with layers of 30, 25, 20, 17.5, 15, 12.5, 10, 7.5, and 5%. The supernatants were carefully layered onto the gradient, and centrifugation was performed at 25,000 rpm using an SW 41 Ti rotor at 4°C for 3 hours. The gradient was divided into 14 equal fractions starting from the top. To precipitate the proteins in these fractions, trichloroacetic acid (10 to 20%) was added and the mixture was incubated at 4°C for 10 min. Subsequently, the samples were centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 5 min, and the resulting pellets were collected and washed twice with 200 μl of cold acetone. For immunoblotting analysis, the collected pellets were dissolved in 2× SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis sample buffer.
Lentivirus production
HEK293 cells cultured in 15-cm dishes with ~80% confluency were cotransfected with 12 μg of a lentiviral vector, along with 9 μg of psPAX2 and 3 μg of pMD2.G (Addgene, #12260 and #12259). After 6 hours, the culture medium was replaced with fresh medium. Following a 48-hour incubation period, the medium was collected and centrifuged at 25,000 rpm at 4°C for 2 hours. Two milliliters of DMEM was added to the viral pellet and then kept at 4°C overnight. The virus pellet was then resuspended, and aliquots were stored at −80°C.
Cell line construction
The pLJM1-Tmem192-mRFP-3xHA vector (#134631) was obtained from Addgene to create a stable cell line expressing TMEM192. HEK293 cells were incubated with lentiviruses containing the Tmem192-mRFP-3xHA coding sequence in the presence of polybrene (2.5 μg/ml). After 24 hours, the infected cells were treated with puromycin (3 μg/ml) to select lentivirus-positive cells. Clonal cell lines were then generated by serial dilution and cultured in 96-well plates. The clonal cell line (HEK192) expressing Tmem192-mRFP-3xHA was confirmed by immunoblotting. In addition, lentiCRISPRv2-Blast– and lentiCRISPRv2-Blast-ITCH–based lentiviruses (
19
) were incubated with RPE1 cells for 48 hours, and the infected cells were treated with blasticidin (30 μg/ml) to select lentivirus-positive cells. Clonal cell lines were derived by serial dilution and culturing in 96-well plates and verified by immunoblot blotting and sequencing.
Lysosome immunoprecipitation
Lysosomes derived from HEK192 cells expressing TMEM192-RFP-3xHA were isolated following established procedures (
78
). In brief, cells were cultured on 150-mm dishes and transfected with indicated vectors. After 48 hours, the cells were rinsed twice with ice-cold KPBS buffer (136 mM KCl and 10 mM KH
2
PO4, pH 7.25) containing a protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich, P8340) and harvested by centrifugation at 1500 rpm for 5 min. The cell pellets were resuspended in 1 ml of KPBS supplemented with 3.6% (w/v) OptiPrep (Sigma-Aldrich, D1556), and the fractionation was performed by passing the suspension through a 23-gauge syringe 10 to 15 times, followed by centrifugation at 2700 rpm for 10 min. The resulting postnuclear supernatant was collected and mixed with 40 μl of prewashed anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88836) with rotation for 30 min. The lysosome-bound beads were washed twice with KPBS (+ OptiPrep) and twice with KPBS. Subsequently, the samples were eluted using a Pierce IgG elution buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 21208) and subjected to immunoblotting analysis.
Dextran degradation assay
HeLa cells were grown on coverslips to 50 to 60% confluence and were then transfected with either wild-type ITCH or the inactivated ITCH-CS. Twenty-four hours later, cells were incubated with AF488-dextran (0.4 mg/ml; 10,000 molecular weight, Invitrogen,
D22910
) for 20 min in culture medium, as previously described (
35

For uptake analysis, the samples were immediately fixed with 4% PFA. For chase analysis, parallel samples were incubated in normal culture medium for 5 hours before fixing them with 4% PFA. The coverslips were mounted using ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant with DAPI (Invitrogen,
P36962
), and images were captured using a confocal microscope (Leica, TCS SP8). AF488-dextran–containing particles in each cell were then calculated.
Proximity ligation assay
PLAs were performed using the mouse/rabbit Duolink In Situ Red Kits (Sigma-Aldrich, DUO92002, DUO92004, and DUO92008). Briefly, cells were seeded onto eight-well glass chamber slides and fixed with 4% PFA in PBS at room temperature for 15 min. The cells were then blocked in the blocking solution at 37°C for 1 hour before being incubated with primary antibodies in an antibody dilution buffer at 4°C overnight. Then, cells were incubated with the PLA probe solution at 37°C for 1 hour, followed by incubation with the ligation solution at 37°C for 30 min, and the amplification solution at 37°C for 100 min. After rinses with 1× and then 0.01× Wash Buffer B, the slides were mounted with coverslips and ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant with DAPI (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
P36971
). The PLA dot signals were imaged using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope.
Protein solubility analysis
The solubility of proteins from mammalian cells was analyzed using previously reported procedures with modifications (
75

HEK293 cells were seeded on 60-mm dishes, and 48 hours after transfection, the cells were rinsed twice with PBS and lysed using 200 μl of a lysis buffer composed of 50 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 1 mM EDTA, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich, P8340), and 25 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich, I6125). The lysates were sonicated on ice for 1 min using a microtip sonicator and then centrifuged in an Airfuge (Beckman Coulter) at 130,000
g
for 5 min to separate insoluble and soluble fractions. The resulting pellets were washed by resuspension in the aforementioned lysis buffer and another centrifugation at 130,000
g
for 5 min. The pellets were resuspended in a urea/SDS buffer (8 M urea, 5% SDS, 40 mM tris-HCl, pH 6.8, and 0.1 mM EDTA) and boiled for 10 min to dissolve the aggregates. The resulting fractions were analyzed using immunoblotting.

Antigen retrieval was performed by incubating the slides in sub-boiling 10 mM citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for 20 min. Subsequently, the sections were incubated with another blocking solution (0.3% Triton X-100, 5% normal donkey serum, and 1% BSA in tris-buffered saline) in a humidified chamber for 1 hour at room temperature. The blocking solution was then aspirated, and the sections were incubated with a primary antibody diluted in the blocking buffer (ITCH, 1:200) overnight at 4°C. The next day, the sections were washed with PBS and treated with biotinylated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Vector Laboratories, BA-1000, 1:500) for 1 hour. Afterward, the signal was detected using 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (Vector Laboratories, K-4100). The sections were rinsed again three times for 10 min in PBS and underwent dehydration with a series of graded alcohols. Last, the sections were cleared with three 5-min incubations in xylene and coverslipped with DPX Mountant (Sigma-Aldrich, 06522).

INTRODUCTION
Protein homeostasis is essential for cellular health and is tightly maintained by protein quality control systems that degrade misfolded proteins (
1
). Perturbation of protein homeostasis is a common theme in neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Although ALS is characterized by motor neuron loss and FTD by progressive cognitive decline, genetic and pathological studies have suggested that these conditions lie on a shared clinical spectrum (
2
). For instance, a hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the
C9orf72
gene represents the most common genetic cause for both ALS and FTD. A common pathology in neurodegenerative diseases is the accumulation of proteinaceous inclusions. In
C9orf72
-linked ALS/FTD, toxic polydipeptide repeats are accumulated in patient tissues (
3
,
4
). Moreover, TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43)–positive inclusions are a pathologic hallmark of ALS, FTD, and a significant subset of AD cases (
5
–
8
). Uncovering the molecular mechanisms that regulate protein quality control and how their dysfunction leads to proteotoxicity is critical to understanding disease pathogenesis.
Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles that mediate the degradation and recycling of various cellular components, including misfolded proteins and damaged organelles (
9
). Within lysosomes, hydrolytic enzymes break down cargo into basic constituents such as amino acids (
10
). The proper targeting of lysosomal hydrolases depends on posttranslational modifications that occur in the Golgi apparatus, such as mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the cis-Golgi network (CGN). This tag is subsequently recognized by receptors in the trans-Golgi network (TGN), guiding the lysosomal hydrolases into the endolysosomal pathway and ensuring their proper delivery to the lysosomes for maturation (
10
). In most mammalian cells, including neurons, the Golgi complex forms a continuous ribbon structure. However, altered organization of the Golgi complex has been recognized as a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases, where the Golgi complex becomes disrupted and breaks into smaller, isolated elements, in a process known as Golgi fragmentation (
11
,
12
). The fragmentation of Golgi has been observed in patients with AD and ALS and animal models (
13
,
14
), and notably, it has been found to occur at an early stage preceding other pathological events (
15
–
17
). Despite the increasing evidence connecting Golgi fragmentation to neurodegenerative diseases, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood (
18
).
Here, we identified E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase Itchy homolog (ITCH), also known as AIP4, as a critical regulator that induces fragmentation of the Golgi networks. ITCH-induced Golgi fragmentation leads to the mislocalization of lysosomal hydrolases sorting factors from the Golgi apparatus to the cytoplasm, resulting in reduced activities of hydrolases in the lysosomes. The impairment in lysosomal functions compromises the clearance of disease-associated misfolded proteins and thus contributes to the proteotoxicity in
Drosophila
and mammalian neuronal models. We also identified USP11 as an upstream regulator that stabilizes ITCH through deubiquitination. The USP11-ITCH axis is abnormally up-regulated in tissues from patients with ALS and AD, suggesting that it may play a role in the pathogenesis of these diseases.
RESULTS
ITCH promotes Golgi fragmentation
Our previous work demonstrated that ITCH regulates the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) life cycle by modulating levels of the Golgi-resident proprotein convertase enzyme furin (
19
), prompting us to investigate the potential function of ITCH in regulating the morphologies of the Golgi apparatus. When ITCH was ectopically expressed in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 and HeLa cells, immunofluorescence (IF) analyses showed that both the CGN and the TGN, as labeled by their marker proteins, 130 kDa cis-Golgi matrix protein 1 (GM130) and trans-Golgi network protein 2 (TGN46), respectively, underwent significant fragmentation and scattering throughout the cell by the increased expression of ITCH (
Fig. 1, A to D
, and fig. S1, A to D). Furthermore, we used a catalytically dead mutant of ITCH carrying the C830S mutation (ITCH-CS) (
20
) and found that it had no impact on the highly ordered, ribbon-like structure of the CGN or TGN, indicating that the activity of ITCH is required for the regulation of the Golgi apparatus (
Fig. 1, A to D
, and fig. S1, A to D). To examine whether this effect is dose dependent, we compared ITCH expression driven by the strong cytomegalovirus (CMV) promoter to expression driven by the weaker interferon-stimulated response element (ISRE) promoter. Cells expressing higher levels of ITCH (CMV) displayed more severe Golgi fragmentation, whereas cells with lower ITCH expression (ISRE) exhibited milder disruption, supporting a dose-dependent relationship between ITCH levels and Golgi integrity (fig. S1E).

Autoinhibition through intramolecular interactions regulates the catalytic activity of neuronal precursor cell-expressed developmentally downregulated 4 (Nedd4)-family E3 ubiquitin ligases, including ITCH (
21
). To determine whether the ectopically expressed ITCH exhibits E3 ligase activity, we assessed overall ubiquitination and ITCH self-ubiquitination in cells expressing either wild-type or inactive ITCH. Wild-type ITCH notably increased polyubiquitinated protein levels in the whole lysate and displayed self-ubiquitination, while the inactive mutant did not, confirming that the ectopic ITCH is functionally active (fig. S1F).
To evaluate whether ITCH specifically affects the Golgi, we examined the structural integrity of other organelles, including the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (calnexin), endosomes [(RAS-associated protein 5 (Rab5)], mitochondria [(translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 (Tom20)], and microtubules (α-tubulin), in HeLa cells expressing either wild-type or mutant ITCH. No significant differences were observed, suggesting that ITCH specifically regulates the Golgi apparatus (fig. S1, G to J). In addition, double staining for Golgi and ER markers showed no substantial fusion between fragmented Golgi and the ER upon elevation of ITCH levels (fig. S1K). To investigate the role of ITCH in regulating Golgi in neurons, we expressed either wild-type ITCH or the inactive ITCH-CS mutant in primary neurons isolated from mouse brains. As in non-neuronal cells, wild-type ITCH, but not the mutant, induced pronounced fragmentation of both CGN and TGN in these neurons (fig. S1L and
Fig. 1, E to H
).
Given that Golgi fragmentation also occurs during apoptosis (
22
), we next examined the Golgi in wild-type and ITCH knockout retinal pigment epithelial (RPE1) cells under apoptosis-inducing conditions to investigate potential involvement of ITCH. Following treatment with the apoptosis inducer camptothecin (
23
), ITCH-deficient cells maintained significantly higher Golgi integrity compared to wild-type controls (fig. S1, M and N). Notably, even in the absence of apoptotic stress, ITCH knockout cells displayed a more compact Golgi structure (fig. S1, M and O), suggesting that ITCH has an intrinsic function in promoting Golgi fragmentation.
To further evaluate ITCH’s role in regulating Golgi structures, we performed subcellular fractionation and analyzed the distributions of the Golgi marker proteins (fig. S1P). The elevated levels of ITCH, but not its inactive form ITCH-CS, shifted GM130 and TGN46, the Golgi marker proteins for the CGN and TGN, respectively, from high-density to the low-density fractions (
Fig. 1, I and J
), consistent with Golgi fragmentation. Conversely, in ITCH knockout cells, the Golgi proteins GM130 and TGN46 shifted in the opposite direction from low-density to high-density fractions (fig. S1, Q and R). As a control, the total protein levels of GM130 or TGN46 remained unchanged under these conditions (fig. S1, S and T), indicating that their shifts in the subcellular fractions reflect changes in Golgi organization rather than changes in protein abundance.
ITCH regulates Golgi sorting factors and lysosomal enzymes
The Golgi membrane-bound
N
-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase is an essential sorting factor that modifies lysosomal enzymes with M6P, a key signal for Golgi-to-lysosome transport (
24
,
25
). N-Acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate transferase subunits alpha and beta (GNPTAB) is the catalytic subunit of the
N
-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase complex. To assess the effect of ITCH on Golgi sorting, we examined GNPTAB localization in HeLa cells expressing either wild-type or catalytically inactive ITCH. In control cells and those expressing ITCH-CS, GNPTAB colocalized with the CGN. However, in cells with elevated levels of wild-type ITCH, GNPTAB signals became diffusely distributed throughout the cytoplasm (
Fig. 2A
), consistent with ITCH-induced Golgi fragmentation. Notably, most of the dispersed GNPTAB did not localize to lysosomes (fig. S2A). Moreover, the elevated ITCH expression did not reduce the total levels of endogenous GNPTAB, and ITCH ablation in the knockout cells did not increase them (fig. S2, B and C), indicating that ITCH-mediated redistribution of GNPTAB is independent of its turnover. We next examined the lysosomal enzyme trafficking factor (LYSET), a Golgi sorting factor required for the Golgi localization of GNPTAB and for Golgi-to-lysosome trafficking of lysosomal enzymes (
26
,
27
). Similar to GNPTAB, LYSET was dispersed from the CGN to the cytoplasm in cells with elevated expression of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS (fig. S2D). Furthermore, the levels of M6P modification were assessed in cells expressing either wild-type or inactive ITCH. Compared to inactive ITCH-CS, cells with elevated wild-type ITCH showed significantly decreased M6P modifications (fig. S2E). Conversely, in ITCH knockout cells, the level of M6P modification was increased (fig. S2F). Together, these data indicate that ITCH-induced Golgi fragmentation disrupts the localization and functions of Golgi sorting factors.

The modification and sorting of lysosomal enzymes in Golgi are critical for their maturation processes. We next examined whether ITCH affects the maturation of lysosomal enzymes. Cathepsin B (CTSB), a cysteine protease and one of the most abundant lysosomal hydrolases in the brain (
28
), undergoes Golgi-mediated sorting and proteolytic processing in lysosomes to convert its pro-form (pro-CTSB) into the mature form (
29
–
31
). To test whether Golgi fragmentation directly affects CTSB maturation, we treated cells with the fungal metabolite brefeldin A or nocodazole, both inducers of Golgi fragmentation (
32
,
33
). These treatments significantly impaired CTSB maturation (fig. S2, G and H). Consistent with the phenotypes of Golgi fragmentation and impaired functions, the elevated levels of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, led to a deficit in the maturation of endogenous CTSB, as indicated by the increase in the pro-CTSB and the decrease in the mature form (
Fig. 2, B to D
). In contrast, in the ITCH knockout cells, the level of pro-CTSB was decreased, along with an increase in the level of mature CTSB (
Fig. 2, E to G
), confirming the negative regulation of CTSB maturation exerted by ITCH. Furthermore, elevated ITCH disrupted the colocalization of CTSB with lysosomal associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1), further supporting impaired trafficking or maturation (fig. S2I). These data indicate that ITCH decreases the effective lysosomal pool of mature hydrolases.
To probe the impact of ITCH on lysosomal functions, we examined the molecular phenotypes of the lysosomes upon the modulation of ITCH. First, we observed that the levels of lysosomal structure proteins, LAMP1 and transmembrane protein 192 (TMEM192), remain unchanged by either elevation or ablation of ITCH (fig. S2, J and K). Accordingly, the levels of LAMP1 fluorescence signals remain consistent upon expression of wild-type or the inactivated form of ITCH (fig. S2L), suggesting that the overall levels of lysosomes were unaltered. Next, we performed subcellular fractionation experiments to examine whether ITCH regulates the density of lysosomes or the distribution of lysosomal enzymes (fig. S1O). Using TMEM192 as a marker to examine the distribution of lysosomes across the fractionated gradients, we observed that elevated levels of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, led to a shift in the population of the lysosomes from the low-density fractions to the high-density fractions (
Fig. 2H
). Furthermore, when the distribution of the lysosomal enzyme CTSB was analyzed in the fractionated gradients, we found that the elevated levels of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, led to a substantial decrease in the level of mature CTSB in the low-density lysosomes but a slight increase of the mature enzyme in the high-density lysosomes (
Fig. 2I
). Together, these data suggest that ITCH promotes the formation of high-density lysosomes, potentially due to cargo accumulation, and compromises the function of normal low-density lysosomes.
Furthermore, we isolated lysosomes by immunoprecipitation from HEK293 cells stably expressing hemagglutinin (HA)–tagged TMEM192 and analyzed the levels of lysosomal proteins (fig. S3A). The elevated levels of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, significantly decreased the level of mature CTSB in the isolated lysosomes, whereas the level of the structural protein LAMP1 was unchanged (
Fig. 2J
). As expected, no pro-CTSB was detected in the isolated lysosomes as it undergoes proteolytic processing during the fusion of late endosomes and lysosomes. Moreover, we generated ITCH knockout cells from the TMEM-expressing line and found that the ITCH ablation led to a significant increase in the level of mature CTSB in the isolated lysosomes (
Fig. 2K
). In addition, the levels of CTSL and CTSD, two other important lysosomal hydrolases, were regulated by ITCH in the same manner as that of CTSB in the isolated lysosomes (fig. S3, B and C). These data support the observations from the imaging and biochemical analyses of intact cells, confirming that ITCH impairs the sorting and maturation of lysosomal enzymes through Golgi disruption.
ITCH inhibits lysosomal degradation of autophagosomal proteins
Autophagy, a crucial degradation system for proteins and other cellular components, relies on the fusion of autophagosome with lysosomes to complete the degradation process (
34
). Given ITCH’s role in regulating lysosomal function, we examined autophagosomal markers microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3B (LC3B) and p62 using IF. The elevated levels of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, significantly increased the quantity and size of LC3B- and p62-positive puncta (
Fig. 3, A and B
, and fig. S3, D and E), suggesting impaired degradation of autophagosomes. Furthermore, we assessed endogenous LC3B levels and observed that the elevated levels of ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, significantly increased the LC3-II/LC3-I (autophagosome/cytosolic LC3) ratio (
Fig. 3C
), consistent with the decreased lysosomal degradative activities. Conversely, in the ITCH knockout cells, the ratio of LC3-II/LC3-I was decreased (
Fig. 3D
). These data indicate that ITCH negatively regulates the autophagy-lysosome system.

We next performed subcellular fractionation to analyze the distribution of autophagosomal and lysosomal proteins. Immunoblotting analysis showed that ITCH, but not the inactive ITCH-CS, promoted the localization of LC3-II in higher density fractions, in accordance with the shift of the lysosomal marker TMEM192 from the low-density to higher-density lysosomes (
Fig. 3, E and F

Fig. 3G

To functionally access lysosomal degradation capacity, we used a pH-insensitive Alexa Fluor 488 (AF488)–dextran probe, which is internalized via endocytosis and degraded in lysosomes (
35
). In a chase experiment to track the degradation of the probe, a large portion of the fluorescence signal was degraded after a 5-hour chase in cells expressing the catalytically inactive ITCH-CS mutant. However, degradation of the probe was significantly slower in cells ectopically expressing wild-type ITCH (
Fig. 3, J and K
), confirming reduced lysosomal degradative activity. Together, these data demonstrate that ITCH inhibits lysosomal degradation of autophagosomal proteins, impairing autophagic clearance that could lead to proteostasis dysfunction.

M337V

38

M337V

M337V
protein. ITCH, but not its inactive form, significantly prolonged the half-life of TDP-43
M337V
protein (
Fig. 4B
), consistent with ITCH acting as a negative regulator of protein quality control.

USP11 interacts with ITCH and positively regulates its level
To investigate the potential dysregulation of ITCH in neurodegeneration, we examined a panel of tissues from patients with ALS using Western blot (WB) analysis and found that ITCH levels were significantly up-regulated in samples from patients with ALS compared to those from non-neurological controls (see below). To identify proteins that regulate ITCH levels, we performed a proteomic analysis of the coimmunoprecipitants pulled down by ITCH (fig. S6A). Among the identified interactors of ITCH, there were several proteins involved in ubiquitination pathways, including seven ubiquitin-specific proteases (USPs), the largest group of deubiquitylating enzymes (DUBs) (fig. S6B). DUBs are proteases that remove ubiquitin moieties from ubiquitylated substrates or poly-ubiquitin chains (
48
). We focused on these USPs since they could be potential positive regulators of ITCH. To assess the roles of these USPs in controlling ITCH levels, we generated stable knockdown or knockout cells lines for BRCA1/BRCA2-containing complex 3 (BRCC3), USP7, USP9x, USP15, USP10, USP11, and USP24 and then analyzed endogenous ITCH protein levels. Fig. 5A
and fig. S6, C to H). In addition, treatment of cells with a small molecule inhibitor of USP11, mitoxantrone (MTX), significantly reduced ITCH protein levels (
Fig. 5B
). As a control, treatment with an inhibitor of USP10, spautin-1 (Sp-1), had no impact on ITCH levels (
Fig. 5B
).

With increased levels of USP11, there was a significant decrease in the levels of ubiquitinated ITCH, whereas the control USPs, including USP15 and BRCC36, did not exhibit any ability to deubiquitinate ITCH (
Fig. 6A
). Using an antibody specifically against K48-linked polyubiquitin chains involved in protein degradation, we observed that USP11, but not the control USPs, displayed the activity to remove K48-linked polyubiquitin chains from ITCH (
Fig. 6B
).

Fig. 7D

Furthermore, IF analysis of the spinal cords revealed Golgi apparatus fragmentation in the motor neurons of patients with ALS, and the number of motor neurons with fragmented Golgi was significantly higher than in the control cases (

DISCUSSION
In the present study, we identify ITCH as a critical regulator of Golgi integrity, lysosomal protein trafficking, and proteotoxicity associated with neurodegenerative diseases. ITCH, but not its inactive form, promotes Golgi fragmentation and leads to mislocalization of lysosomal hydrolase sorting factors, such as GNPTAB and LYSET, from the Golgi to the cytoplasm. Consequently, the maturation of lysosomal hydrolases, such as CTSB, is impaired during its trafficking from Golgi to the lysosome, leading to reduced lysosomal functions. As a result, ITCH hinders the clearance of disease-associated misfolded proteins, including TDP-43, and exacerbates their proteotoxic effects. We further show that USP11 deubiquitinates ITCH and enhances its stability. The up-regulation of the USP11-ITCH axis in patients with ALS and AD implicates this previously unrecognized pathway in the pathogenesis of these neurodegenerative diseases (
Fig. 7G
).
Golgi fragmentation and proteotoxic imbalance are both common features of neurodegenerative diseases (
11
–
14
,
51
,
52
), with the Golgi-associated changes considered as early-stage events in the pathogenic cascades (
15
–
17
). Our findings demonstrate that the accumulation of the ubiquitin E3 ligase ITCH is a critical driver for both Golgi fragmentation and heightened proteotoxicity. ITCH-induced Golgi fragmentation may represent a stress response common to diverse neurodegenerative conditions. The impaired autophagy-lysosomal pathway, as a result from the ITCH-mediated Golgi fragmentation, prevents the efficient clearance of misfolded proteins, exacerbating the cellular dysfunction observed in
Drosophila
and mammalian neurons. The integrity of Golgi structures is crucial for various other cellular processes, including protein and lipid processing as well as the synthesis of essential cellular components (
53
–
57
). Thus, the ITCH-induced Golgi fragmentation may lead to other cellular deficits, such as aberrant protein and lipid modifications, mislocalization of molecules, and disturbance in vesicle transport. Future research is needed to fully understand the multifaceted impact of ITCH dysregulation on cellular homeostasis and its implication in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.
Given the abnormal accumulation of ITCH in patients with ALS and AD, we examined the upstream regulators of ITCH and identified USP11 as a key positive regulator of ITCH protein stability. As a deubiquitinase, USP11 catalyzes the removal of polyubiquitin chains, including the K48-linked chains as signals for protein degradation, from ITCH, thereby increasing its stability. Notably, USP11 is also up-regulated in patients with ALS and AD, and its levels strongly correlate with those of ITCH, establishing the USP11-ITCH axis as a dysregulated and disease-relevant pathway. As ITCH up-regulation was observed in neurons, tissue- or cell-specific approaches, such as gene editing using specific promoters, could be developed in the future when considering USP11-ITCH axis as a therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases.
The identification of ITCH as a crucial regulator of Golgi integrity may have broad implications in understanding the underlying mechanisms of neurodegeneration, given the observation of Golgi fragmentation in multiple diseases from ALS and AD to Parkinson’s disease (
52
,
58
–
66
). Furthermore, ITCH may affect proteotoxicity associated with a range of diseases, as it acts as a regulator of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. ITCH depletion protects against diverse misfolded proteins in
Drosophila
and mammalian neurons, suggesting its potential as a wide-spectrum antiproteotoxicity target. Furthermore, in a separate study, we found that ITCH plays a central role in the life cycle of SARS-CoV-2 by regulating the viral assembly and secretion and that ITCH is robustly activated by SARS-CoV-2 infection (
19
). Given emerging evidence linking SARS-CoV-2 infection to neurodegenerative diseases such as AD and ALS (
67
–
73
), our findings offer a potential mechanistic bridge between viral infection and neurodegeneration. In summary, our study reveals ITCH as a regulator of Golgi architecture, lysosomal function, and proteotoxicity. The dysregulated USP11-ITCH axis may contribute to the pathogenesis of several relevant neurodegenerative diseases.

The expression vectors pRK5-SOD1
G85R
and pRK5-TDP-43
M337V

–

Cell lines and cell transfection
Human retinal pigment epithelial cells [RPE1; hTERT-RPE1, American Type Culture Collection (ATCC), CRL-4000] were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM)/F-12, GlutaMAX supplement (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10565042) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, A5256701); HEK293 cells (ATCC, CRL-3216) and HeLa cells (ATCC, CCL-2) were cultured in DMEM (Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A5256701); and all cell lines were authenticated by short tandem repeat analysis. Transfection was performed with a mixture of plasmid DNAs and the cationic polymer linear polyethylenimine (Polysciences, 593215) when cells reached a confluence of ~40 to 60%.
Immunoprecipitation
Cells were collected and lysed in a solution that contained the following components: protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich, P8340), 50 mM tris-HCl (with a pH of 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, and 0.2% NP-40. After incubating for 1 hour at 4°C, a brief period of sonication was performed using a microtip, followed by centrifugation of the samples at 12,000
g
for 10 min at 4°C. The resulting supernatants were then combined with a primary antibody and Protein A/G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88803), and the mixture was incubated overnight at 4°C. Then, the samples underwent five rounds of rinsing using a wash buffer composed of 50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.2% NP-40. The collected precipitates were released by IgG elution buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 21028). For Flag-based immunoprecipitation, the precipitated proteins were released from the beads using a lysis buffer containing the 3× Flag peptide (Sigma-Aldrich, catalog number F4799).
For the denaturing precipitation-immunoblotting analysis of ubiquitination, cells were treated with 300 μl of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution containing 1% SDS and boiled for 10 min. Subsequently, the lysates were diluted 1:3 using PBS and sonicated for 1 min using a microtip sonicator. The lysates were centrifuged at a speed of 12,000
g
for 10 min. The resulting supernatants were then diluted five times with PBS. These diluted supernatants were incubated with Flag-antibody beads overnight at 4°C. After five washes with PBS buffer containing 0.2% NP-40, the proteins were released from the beads using lysis buffer containing the 3× Flag peptide.
Golgi quantification
To quantify cis- and trans-Golgi structures, we conducted IF analysis on various cells using antibodies against GM130, TGN38, and TGN46. The integrity of the Golgi was assessed by classifying GM130, TGN38, and TGN46 signals into five levels. The assigned values (1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, and 0) reflect the Golgi integrity for each cell, with an intact Golgi receiving a score of 1 and a completely smeared Golgi scoring 0. Over 30 cells in each group were classified for this assessment.
Human and mouse tissues
Tau4R-AP transgenic mice have been described previously (
50
), and details of the human tissues are provided in tables S1 and S2. Tissue extracts from mouse brains, spinal cords from patients with ALS, and brains from patients with AD were prepared according to established protocols (
45
). Briefly, the tissues were first washed with cold PBS. Then, they were homogenized using glass tissue grinders in cold radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer consisting of 50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1% SDS, 100 mM sodium fluoride, 17.5 mM β-glycerophosphate, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 10% glycerol, and EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). The resulting homogenates were centrifuged at a speed of 1000
g
at 4°C for 10 min. The supernatants were further centrifuged at 16,000
g
for an additional 10 min. The final supernatants were collected and used for subsequent immunoblotting analysis.
Mass spectrometry
For the identification of the ITCH interactome, HEK293 cells were transfected with the vectors expressing Flag-tagged ITCH for 2 days. Then, the cells were collected and lysed. Flag immunoprecipitation was performed following the procedure described above. The precipitates in elution buffer (PBS containing 3× Flag peptides) were subjected to reduction, alkylation, and trypsin digestion. The resulting peptides were analyzed using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The proteomic data were searched against the SwissProt human database using MASCOT software to identify the interacting proteins. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE (
77
) partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD057324.
IF analysis
Twenty-four hours after transfection, cells were washed twice with PBS and then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 min at room temperature. Following the fixation, cells were washed three times with PBS and then permeabilized and blocked using PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) at room temperature for 1 hour. Then, the cells were incubated with the primary antibody at 4°C overnight. After three washes, cells were incubated with the fluorescently conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 hour. Last, coverslips were mounted using ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant, which contains 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
P36971
).
Cell fractionation
Cells were washed with PBS and then suspended in a cold homogenization buffer (0.25 M sucrose, 1 mM EDTA, and 10 mM Hepes, pH 7.4). The suspension was passed repeatedly through a 23-gauge syringe needle to disrupt the cells. After centrifuging the homogenates at 1000
g
for 10 min at 4°C to remove the nuclei and undisrupted cells, the supernatants were collected to isolate the membrane fractions using density gradient ultracentrifugation. Discontinuous gradients of iodixanol were prepared using OptiPrep (Accurate Chemical and Scientific, Westbury, NY), with layers of 30, 25, 20, 17.5, 15, 12.5, 10, 7.5, and 5%. The supernatants were carefully layered onto the gradient, and centrifugation was performed at 25,000 rpm using an SW 41 Ti rotor at 4°C for 3 hours. The gradient was divided into 14 equal fractions starting from the top. To precipitate the proteins in these fractions, trichloroacetic acid (10 to 20%) was added and the mixture was incubated at 4°C for 10 min. Subsequently, the samples were centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 5 min, and the resulting pellets were collected and washed twice with 200 μl of cold acetone. For immunoblotting analysis, the collected pellets were dissolved in 2× SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis sample buffer.
Lentivirus production
HEK293 cells cultured in 15-cm dishes with ~80% confluency were cotransfected with 12 μg of a lentiviral vector, along with 9 μg of psPAX2 and 3 μg of pMD2.G (Addgene, #12260 and #12259). After 6 hours, the culture medium was replaced with fresh medium. Following a 48-hour incubation period, the medium was collected and centrifuged at 25,000 rpm at 4°C for 2 hours. Two milliliters of DMEM was added to the viral pellet and then kept at 4°C overnight. The virus pellet was then resuspended, and aliquots were stored at −80°C.

). In brief, cells were cultured on 150-mm dishes and transfected with indicated vectors. After 48 hours, the cells were rinsed twice with ice-cold KPBS buffer (136 mM KCl and 10 mM KH

Immunohistochemistry
Paraffin sections were deparaffinized using xylene and rehydrated through graded ethanol. Antigen retrieval was performed by incubating the slides in sub-boiling 10 mM citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for 20 min. The sections were then cooled to room temperature and underwent three 5-min washes with PBS before being incubated in a 3% H
2
O
2
solution for 15 min. Afterward, the sections were washed twice with PBS and incubated with a serum-free blocking buffer (ScyTek, 61886) for 10 min. Subsequently, the sections were incubated with another blocking solution (0.3% Triton X-100, 5% normal donkey serum, and 1% BSA in tris-buffered saline) in a humidified chamber for 1 hour at room temperature. The blocking solution was then aspirated, and the sections were incubated with a primary antibody diluted in the blocking buffer (ITCH, 1:200) overnight at 4°C. The next day, the sections were washed with PBS and treated with biotinylated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Vector Laboratories, BA-1000, 1:500) for 1 hour. The tissues were then rinsed with PBS and incubated with ABC reagent (Vector Laboratories, PK-7100) for 30 min. Afterward, the signal was detected using 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (Vector Laboratories, K-4100). The sections were rinsed again three times for 10 min in PBS and underwent dehydration with a series of graded alcohols. Last, the sections were cleared with three 5-min incubations in xylene and coverslipped with DPX Mountant (Sigma-Aldrich, 06522).
